95: The network architecture of a digital two-way radio system shall comprise the service module, the signal source, the distributed antenna system (DAS) and the digital terminals (Figure 4.1.1).
97: Service function units shall be selected and configured according to the required functionality, so as to provide extended communication or management functions beyond voice calling. Service functions shall comply with Chapter 5 of this reference.
99: The signal source shall comprise base stations or repeaters, the combiner platform and system monitoring, and may adopt a networked signal-source architecture (Figure 4.2.1).
100: The interface between the signal source and an active DAS shall be a single RF port carrying combined transmit and receive paths.
101: The signal source shall provide system monitoring functions, in accordance with Chapter 5 of this reference.
104: Active and passive distributed antenna systems should meet the following requirements:
105: An active DAS should comprise bi-directional amplifiers (BDAs) or fiber-optic BDAs, a point of interface (POI) and the antenna and feeder subsystem.
106: A passive DAS should comprise a POI and the antenna and feeder subsystem.
107: Radio coverage of a designated area is delivered through the DAS. Where the coverage footprint has to be extended, an active DAS should be used, extending coverage by means of BDAs or fiber-optic BDAs.
108: Where an active DAS is adopted, either a BDA topology or a fiber-optic-repeater topology may be selected, and the following shall apply:
109: Where BDAs are arranged in a tree topology (Figure 4.3.3-1), the signal-source feed may be taken through signal distribution and delivered to the antenna and feeder subsystem after amplification.
110: Where analogue fiber-optic BDAs are used, a star topology between OMUs and ORUs shall be adopted (Figure 4.3.3-2).
112: Where digital fiber-optic BDAs are used, a cascaded or ring topology between OMUs and ORUs may be adopted (Figure 4.3.3-3).
114: A hybrid topology combining BDAs and fiber-optic BDAs may be used where project conditions require it.
116: The antenna and feeder subsystem shall be configured as follows:
117: It consists of couplers and splitters, RF coaxial cable, leaky coaxial (radiating) cable, optical fiber cable and antennas.
119: Equipment shall be selected to suit the indoor or outdoor application environment, and shall comply with the following:
120: for indoor areas and enclosed underground areas, a low-power multi-antenna arrangement should be used;
121: for open outdoor areas, single-point or multi-point outdoor antennas should be used;
122: for tunnels and long, narrow enclosed underground areas, leaky coaxial cable should be used.
124: Where several systems share the antenna and feeder subsystem of one coverage area, a POI shall be used to combine the signals of those systems onto the shared antenna and feeder subsystem (Figure 4.3.5).
268: The composition of the DAS shall comply with Chapter 4 of this reference.
269: The DAS should be designed with products and cable routes suited to the internal structure of the building, the environmental conditions and the coverage requirement, so as to minimise the impact on building structure and finishes.
271: Signal quality across the area covered by the DAS shall comply with the following:
272: the received signal strength at 95% of locations within the coverage area shall be not less than -95 dBm;
273: the received signal strength at 95% of locations in plant rooms, substations and other electrified areas (signal-interference areas) shall be not less than -85 dBm;
274: the carrier-to-noise ratio (CNR) throughout the coverage area shall be not less than 12 dB;
275: output power at radiating points shall be set appropriately, and the maximum radiated field strength at a radiating point shall comply with the applicable EMF exposure limits. 278: The capacity and carrying capability of the DAS shall be sufficient to support normal system operation.
280: Extension of the coverage area shall be achieved by means of BDAs or fiber-optic BDAs.
281: The network topology of BDAs and fiber-optic BDAs shall comply with Section 4.3 of this reference.

8: It covers the design, installation, testing, acceptance and operation and maintenance of two-way radio communication systems and emergency-responder radio communication systems in new-build, renovation and extension projects in industrial and civil buildings. It does not cover VHF maritime mobile radio systems.

15: **Two-way radio in-building communication system** — a system providing digital two-way radio communication service over dedicated 150 MHz, 400 MHz and 350 MHz bands using two-frequency (duplex) networking, comprising the service module, the signal source, the distributed antenna system and the digital terminals.
16: **Security and emergency communication** — dedicated two-way radio communication used for emergency response command and management in the event of an incident, and for routine patrol and enforcement duties.
17: **Signal source** — the radio transmit/receive system comprising base stations or repeaters, the combiner platform and system monitoring.
18: **Base station** — dedicated digital two-way radio equipment with an external antenna, used as the central station.
19: **Repeater** — equipment with an external antenna port used to relay digital signals and boost power, so extending the communication range.
20: **Combiner platform** — equipment, or a combination of equipment, that consolidates several signals on different frequencies within the same band, so that the signals are combined and transmitted over a shared transmit/receive feeder while interference between the frequencies is suppressed. It typically comprises RF combiners, multi-couplers, duplexers and filters.
21: **Distributed antenna system (DAS)** — either active or passive. An active DAS comprises antennas, feeders, couplers, splitters, a point of interface (POI) and BDAs (or fiber-optic BDAs). A passive DAS comprises mainly the antenna and feeder subsystem and a POI.
22: **Bi-directional amplifier (BDA)** — amplifying equipment used where signal power has fallen too low to meet the coverage requirement. Where the signal-source power alone cannot achieve the required coverage, the BDA amplifies it so that a larger area is covered.
23: **Fiber-optic BDA (optical fiber repeater)** — equipment that amplifies the RF signal on the same frequency, acting as a relay between the base station and the digital terminals. It consists principally of an optical fiber master unit (OMU), optical fiber, and an optical fiber remote unit (ORU); RF signals are carried between OMU and ORU over optical fiber. Fiber-optic BDAs are either analogue or digital.
24: **Antenna and feeder subsystem** — the distributed bi-directional radio transmission network formed by antennas, passive components (couplers, splitters, hybrids and the like) and RF cable.
25: **Leaky coaxial (radiating) cable** — cable that both carries the signal and acts as an antenna: through controlled apertures in the outer conductor it radiates and receives electromagnetic energy evenly along its length, providing coverage in areas that would otherwise be radio blind spots.
26: **Coupler / splitter** — an RF signal branching device used to divide the RF signal; includes power splitters and directional couplers.
27: **Point of interface (POI)** — equipment, or a combination of equipment, that combines the downlink signals of several systems onto a shared antenna and feeder subsystem and divides the received uplink signal back out to the respective signal sources or BDAs.
28: **Digital terminal** — the terminal equipment used for two-way radio communication; includes digital portable radios and digital mobile radios.
29: **Digital portable radio** — a digital terminal with an external antenna port, designed to be carried or worn by an individual and powered by an internal battery.
30: **Digital mobile radio** — a digital terminal with an external antenna port, normally installed in a vehicle or vessel or at a fixed position and powered from that installation.
31: **Redundant backup** — two devices or modules that back each other up, so that if one fails the other takes over automatically and immediately.
32: **Digital trunking** — a communication mode using digital technology to share frequency resources and channel service, in which all available channels in the system are shared by all digital terminals and channels are selected automatically.
33: **Push-to-talk (PTT)** — a communication method in which a switch is pressed to change between transmit and receive; commonly used in half-duplex operation.
34: **Group call late entry** — where a digital terminal was unable to join a group call at set-up (because it was switched off or out of service area), the user may join the group call already in progress once the radio is switched on or re-enters coverage.
35: **Authentication** — the process of confirming that a mobile radio, portable radio, base station or repeater is a legitimate member of the system.
36: **Kill / stun / revive** — kill is the process of disabling a mobile or portable radio over the air interface, after which it cannot be re-enabled over the air; stun is the process of disabling a mobile or portable radio over the air interface; revive is the process of re-enabling it over the air interface.
37: **System and equipment monitoring** — technology for monitoring and controlling the system and its equipment, providing real-time status management through alarm management, log management, signalling trace, probes and diagnostic tests.
38: **Carrier-to-noise ratio (CNR)** — the ratio of the wanted carrier power to the RF noise power at the receiver input.
39: **Passive intermodulation (PIM)** — the generation of spurious signals when two or more frequencies mix in a non-linear component.
40: **Insertion loss** — the signal loss introduced by inserting a cable or component between transmitter and receiver.
41: **Voltage standing wave ratio (VSWR)** — the ratio between the voltage amplitude at a standing-wave antinode and that at a node.
42: **Isolation** — the measure of the interference-suppression provided to minimise the effect of interference on the receiver.
43: **Channel spacing** — the difference between the nominal carrier frequencies of two adjacent channels.
44: **Noise-floor control** — controlling the uplink gain of the BDA so as to avoid raising the noise floor of the base station or repeater at the signal source, which would otherwise degrade its sensitivity.
45: **Bit error ratio (BER)** — the ratio, over a given period, of the number of bits received in error to the total number of bits received.
